title: Agentic HIL test reactor configuration
$comment: Additions this schema marks `x-since-version` belong to that plan format version and later. A plan is held to what its own `version:` contains, so a version 2 plan reaching for a version 3 action or key is refused by name rather than quietly accepted here and rejected by an older install elsewhere.

version.description: Format version. Version 1 addressed a `device:` naming a modelled unit that no longer exists. Version 2 routes each step by the section it drives (`debugger` / `port_id` / `bus_id`). Version 3 adds `device:` as the one routing key for every step, the `comparator:` object on feedback actions (a serial line's on `uart_read`, a bus's on `can_read`), `uart_write`, `uart_read` and `delay`, and makes explicit close steps optional. Version 4 adds the `repeat` block step, which runs a nested subset of steps by count or by wall time. Version 5 adds the `read_symbol` action and the numeric `comparator:` it carries, which is the first claim in this format about a value in target memory rather than about text a device sent.

steps.description: A sequence of steps, executed in order and stopped at the first one that fails. The nested sequence of a `repeat` block is the same shape as the plan's own, which is what makes a block step nestable.

device.description: Name of the configured entry this step drives — a `debuggers`, `com_ports` or `can_buses` entry. The one routing key of format version 3: the configuration knows which section a name belongs to, so the step does not have to spell it. The version 2 keys below stay valid as readable aliases; a step writes one or the other, never both.

debugger.description: Name of a debuggers.<name> entry. Optional when the project configures exactly one debugger; required when it configures several.

path.description: A file this step reads or writes. A relative path resolves against `workspace_root`, and no permission relaxes containment: a traversal segment, or a path that resolves outside the workspace by any route including a link, is refused before the run starts rather than on a board that is already halted.

symbol.description: The name of a symbol in the flashed image, in the one spelling every symbol tool here accepts. A plan may name only a symbol the bench allows: `debug.allowed_symbols` is the operator's statement about what may be read off this board, and a step naming anything outside it is refused before the run starts unless the configuration sets `debug.allow_all_symbols`.

timeout.description: How long this step waits, in seconds. Zero is allowed here and asks for no wait at all, which is a reading a step can have when waiting is not the whole of what it does. A step that exists in order to wait refuses zero instead, and says so on its own `timeout_s`.

positiveTimeout.description: A deadline a step waits out. Zero is refused rather than read as 'do not wait': a step whose whole purpose is to wait has no useful reading of no time at all.

comparator.description: What a feedback step claims about what it received. An object rather than a bare value on purpose: the preprocessing a bench eventually needs — scaling a raw count into a unit, converting a base — is addable here as further keys without invalidating a plan written today. None of that exists yet. Exactly one of `equals` and `pattern` says what to look for; `range` narrows a `pattern` capture to a numeric interval. The claim is judged against everything read so far, so output that arrives in pieces still counts, and a step whose claim is never met fails with the tail of what the port did say.

equals.description: The value the output must equal — not merely contain. A serial line has no end, so this is read two ways: any one complete line of what was received matches as soon as its terminator arrives, and the whole of what was received matches on the last pass, once the step's timeout has run out and nothing further is coming. Surrounding whitespace is removed either way. A value the board never terminates therefore costs the full timeout, because until then it cannot be told apart from a value still arriving. Mutually exclusive with `pattern`.

pattern.description: A Python regular expression the output must match, with `re.search` semantics: it is anchored where it is written and nowhere else, so write `^` or `$` when the position is part of the claim. A pattern that does not compile is refused before the run starts. Mutually exclusive with `equals`.

range.description: Inclusive bounds the number captured by `pattern`'s one capture group must fall inside. The pattern must have exactly one capture group, which is refused before the run starts when it does not. A step that times out reports the last value it did capture against these bounds, so a reading that was merely out of range and a board that said nothing read differently.

canComparator.description: Which frame a `can_read` step requires: an identifier filter and a claim about the payload, in the same vocabulary a serial comparator uses. `id` is mandatory because a bus carries every node's traffic — a payload matched without saying whose frame it was is a green another ECU can produce. Frames are judged one at a time as they arrive, never concatenated: a frame is a complete unit, so there is no half-arrived value to wait out and no seam to match across. A step whose claim is never met fails with the tail of the frames the bus did carry, so a wrong identifier and a silent bus read differently.

id.description: The identifier of the frame this step is waiting for, as an integer or a hexadecimal string such as `0x123`. Matched exactly unless `id_mask` widens it.

id_mask.description: A bit mask making the identifier a family rather than one value: a frame matches when `frame_id & mask` equals `id & mask`. This is how a plan waits for any frame of a protocol that encodes a node or a priority in the low bits of the identifier.

extended.description: Which frame namespace the identifier lives in. A standard 0x123 and an extended 0x123 are two different frames on the wire, so a comparator matches only frames of the type it names: the identifier alone does not select across the namespaces. Defaults to `false`, so a comparator that does not say waits for a standard frame; set it `true` to wait for the extended twin.

equals.description: The exact payload bytes the frame must carry, as hexadecimal. Whitespace and case are ignored, so `01 FF` and `01ff` are the same claim. The empty string is the claim that the frame carries no data at all. Mutually exclusive with `pattern`.

pattern.description: A Python regular expression matched against the payload rendered as lowercase hexadecimal without separators, with `re.search` semantics: it is anchored where it is written and nowhere else, so write `^` or `$` when the byte position is part of the claim. A pattern that does not compile is refused before the run starts. Mutually exclusive with `equals`.

range.description: Inclusive bounds the number captured by `pattern`'s one capture group must fall inside. The capture is read as hexadecimal, because what the pattern is matching against is the payload written in hexadecimal: `pattern: "^01(..)"` with `range: {min: 20, max: 30}` says the second byte of that frame is between 20 and 30, with the bounds in decimal as every number in a plan is. The pattern must have exactly one capture group, which is refused before the run starts when it does not. A step that times out reports the last value it did capture against these bounds, so a signal that was merely out of range and a bus that never carried the frame read differently.

symbolComparator.description: What a `read_symbol` step claims about the number a symbol holds. Its own vocabulary rather than the `comparator:` the feedback actions carry: that one judges text and reads a `range` out of a regular expression's capture group, and there is no text in a word of target memory. The claim is made against the integer `debug_symbol_value` decodes the bytes into, which exists only at 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes, so a plan claiming a number at any other width is refused rather than judged. Exactly one of `equals` and `range` says what the value must be, and `mask` beside `equals` makes the claim about bits instead of about the whole word. Nothing here waits: a halted target's memory does not change under the step, so the value is read once and judged once, and an unmet claim fails at once carrying the value it read.

equals.description: The value the symbol must hold, exactly. Beside `mask` it is what the masked bits must hold instead. A YAML plan may write it in hexadecimal (`0x2a`) where that is how the firmware reads; it is the same number either way, and a JSON plan writes the decimal. Mutually exclusive with `range`.

range.description: Inclusive bounds the value must fall inside. Integers, because the reading they bound is one: a symbol holds bytes, and the number those bytes decode to has no fractional part for a bound to sit between. Mutually exclusive with `equals`, and therefore never combined with `mask`.

mask.description: The bits the claim is about: the step compares `value & mask` against `equals`, which is how a plan asserts one flag of a status word without stating every other bit of it. Applied to the unsigned reading, because a mask selects bits while a sign is a reading of the whole width; that is why `signed` is refused beside it rather than quietly ignored. The report carries both the value read and the masked value it was judged on.

signed.description: Which of the two integer readings this claim is about. `debug_symbol_value` returns `value_unsigned` and `value_signed` because the same bytes are honestly both, and above the top bit the two disagree, so a plan asserting a counter that can go negative says so here instead of writing the two's complement of the number it means. Defaults to false, which is the reading `hex` shows in memory order.

location.description: Where the breakpoint goes, written one of four ways: a bare symbol name, `{symbol: <name>}`, `{function: <name>}`, or `{file: <path>, line: <number>}`. The first three name something `debug.allowed_symbols` has to carry, exactly as a dump does. The fourth names no symbol at all, so it is refused unless the configuration sets `debug.allow_all_symbols`: a file and a line can be made to stand anywhere in the image, and an allowlist that a line number walks around is not one. Every breakpoint the reactor sets is removed again after the step, passed or failed.

flash.description: Program the target through the named debugger, exactly as the `flash_firmware` tool does: the same `permissions.allow_flash` on that probe, the same artifact validation, and the same refusal while `allow_raw_debugger_commands` or `allow_mass_erase` is true on it.

image_path.description: The firmware to program. Held to `artifacts.allowed_roots` and `artifacts.allowed_extensions` where `validation` requires them, hashed, and staged privately before the backend sees it, all before the run starts.

reset_after_flash.description: Whether the target is reset once the image is on it. Flashing on its own leaves the board where the backend left it, so a plan that expects a fresh boot asks for one here. It additionally requires `permissions.allow_reset` on the same probe.

reset.description: Reset the target through the named debugger, exactly as the `reset_target` tool does. A backend that cannot run the requested mode refuses it with its own `not_supported`; the step reports that refusal unchanged.

mode.description: How the target is left afterwards. 'run' resets and lets the target execute. 'halt' leaves the core stopped. 'init' additionally runs the target's reset-init event script and is OpenOCD-only.

uartOpen.description: Open a configured serial line for this plan, exactly as `com_session_start` opens it. Every later `uart_write`, `uart_read` and `uart_expect` on that line runs inside this session, and a plan that reads a line it never opened is refused before the run starts. The line stays open across a `repeat` block's iterations.

clear_buffer.description: Discard whatever the line buffered before this step, so what a later read matches came from this run rather than from a previous one. Opening a port a plan may not read is already refused, so the clear this asks for is always permitted here.

uartWrite.description: Serial stimulus on a line this plan opened, exactly as the `com_write` tool sends it. Requires permissions.allow_write on the port, which is refused by name before the run starts. Exactly one of `text` and `hex` says what to send.

text.description: Text to send, encoded with the port's configured encoding. Write the line ending the firmware expects — nothing is appended for you.

hex.description: Raw bytes to send, as hexadecimal. Use this when the stimulus is a protocol frame rather than text.

uartRead.description: Read a serial line this plan has opened. With a `comparator:` the step reads until the claim is met or its timeout passes, reporting the tail of what the port did say when it is not. Without one it is a plain read of whatever the session has, answered exactly as `com_read` answers it.

uartExpect.description: Wait for output on a serial line this plan has opened. Reads the port the same way `com_read` does and matches against everything read so far, so output that arrives in pieces still counts. A step whose expectation never appears fails with the tail of what the port did say. Exactly one of `text` and `pattern` says what to wait for: a step carrying both, or neither, is refused before the run starts. Version 3 spells the same thing as `uart_read` with a `comparator:`, which also carries ranges; this action stays valid.

text.description: The substring the port's output must contain. Mutually exclusive with `pattern`.

pattern.description: A Python regular expression the port's output must match, with `re.search` semantics: it is anchored where it is written and nowhere else, so write `^` or `$` when the position is part of the claim. Use this to check that the board answered with the right value — a counter, a measurement, a version string — rather than merely that it answered. A pattern that does not compile is refused before the run starts. Mutually exclusive with `text`.

uartClose.description: Close a serial line this plan opened. Optional from version 3 on: end-of-run cleanup closes every session the run opened, whether the plan said so or not. Keep an explicit close where the plan means to close, reconfigure and reopen the line mid-run.

canOpen.description: Open a configured CAN bus for this plan, exactly as `can_session_start` opens it. Every later `can_send` and `can_read` on that bus runs inside this session, and a plan that reads a bus it never opened is refused before the run starts. The session stays open across a `repeat` block's iterations.

clear_rx_queue.description: Drain the receive queue before the plan reads. Requires permissions.allow_read on the bus.

canClose.description: Close a CAN bus session this plan opened. Optional from version 3 on, for the same reason `uart_close` is.

canSend.description: One classic CAN frame on a bus this plan opened. Refused before the run on a bus configured `listen_only: true`, which is the claim that observing it sends nothing.

frame_id.description: The identifier this frame carries, as an integer or a hexadecimal string such as `0x123`. The two spellings are the same number; the string is there because a protocol document writes identifiers in hexadecimal and a plan should be diffable against it.

extended.description: Which identifier namespace the frame is sent in. A standard 0x123 and an extended 0x123 are two different frames on the wire, so a receiver waiting for one never sees the other.

rtr.description: Send a remote transmission request, which asks another node for that identifier's data rather than carrying any of its own.

data_hex.description: The payload, as hexadecimal. Whitespace and case are ignored, so `01 FF` and `01ff` are the same two bytes. Defaults to the empty string, which sends a frame carrying no data.

canRead.description: Read a CAN bus this plan has opened. With a `comparator:` the step reads until a frame meets the claim or its `timeout_s` passes, reporting the tail of the frames the bus did carry when none does. Without one it is a plain read of whatever the session has, answered exactly as `can_read` answers it.

max_frames.description: Defaults to the bus's configured max_buffer_frames, which is also the ceiling. With a `comparator:` this is how many frames one read drains, not how many the step may look at: it reads again until the claim is met or the deadline passes.

timeout_s.description: How long the step waits for a frame meeting its `comparator:`. Belongs to the step rather than to one read, which is why it is refused beside `wait_timeout_s`: with a comparator each read waits out whatever is left of this deadline.

wait_timeout_s.description: How long a plain read waits for frames. Without a `comparator:` this is the whole of the step's waiting; with one, name `timeout_s` instead.

debugStart.description: Open this plan's one debug session, exactly as the `debug_start_session` tool does. Every typed debug step below runs inside it and on the debugger that started it; the plan needs no explicit `debug_stop`, because end-of-run cleanup closes the session whether the plan reached that step or a step before it failed. Typed debug sessions are OpenOCD's, and the other backends refuse them with `not_supported`.

image_path.description: The ELF the session resolves symbols out of. It has to be an `.elf` whatever the configured artifact extensions allow, because a session without debug information has no symbol to break on or read.

mode.description: What the session does to the target as it opens. 'attach' takes the board as it is. 'reset_halt' resets it and holds the core stopped, which is how a plan reaches a symbol that is written before main. 'load' additionally writes the image through the session.

runUntilBreakpoint.description: Set one breakpoint, let the target run, and wait for it to stop there. A stop somewhere else is reported as the stop reason it was rather than as a pass, and a target that never arrives fails at `timeout_s`. The breakpoint is removed afterwards either way, so a plan leaves none behind.

dumpMemory.description: Write what one allowed symbol holds to a file, as Intel HEX, exactly as the `debug_dump_symbol_ihex` tool writes it: the same allowlist and the same `debug.max_dump_size_bytes` ceiling. This is how a plan keeps a buffer for something outside the run to look at; `read_symbol` is what claims a value inside the run.

output_path.description: Where the bytes are written. Held to the workspace like every path here, and to a `.hex` or `.ihex` extension, before the run starts. Its parent directory has to exist already; this step creates no directories.

readSymbol.description: Read what one allowed symbol currently holds, through the debug session this plan has open, exactly as the `debug_symbol_value` tool reads it: the same allowlist, the same `debug.max_dump_size_bytes` ceiling applied to the resolved size before any memory is read, and the same resolution, which asks the image's debug information first and falls back to the ELF's own symbol table where there is no type to work with, so an assembly-defined object is readable too. With a `comparator:` the step judges the number the bytes decode to and fails naming the value it read; without one it is a plain read, answered exactly as the tool answers it, which is how a plan records a value it does not want to assert. This is the format's first claim about target memory rather than about what a device sent, and it is deliberately not a wait: there is no `timeout_s` here, because a halted target's memory does not change under the step.

size_bytes.description: The width this plan expects the symbol to have, in bytes, which the step asserts against the width the target actually resolves it at: a firmware that turned a `uint32_t` into a `uint16_t` fails the step rather than having its new value judged as if nothing had moved. Stating it is also what lets two refusals be earned before the run instead of on the bench, because the width is then known without asking a board: a width above this bench's `debug.max_dump_size_bytes`, and a width beside a `comparator:` that is not 1, 2, 4 or 8. Leave it out and the plan is judged on both counts at runtime instead, where the resolved size is finally known, with a stated reason either way.

debugStop.description: Close the debug session on the debugger that started it. Optional, for the reason `uart_close` and `can_close` are: end-of-run cleanup closes it anyway. Keep an explicit stop where the plan means to close the session and go on doing something else with the board.

delay.description: Wait, driving nothing. Served by every device kind, so the step names the device the plan is waiting on and appears in the run's result like any other step — a wait that left no trace would be a gap in the record of what a test did. Prefer a read with a `comparator:` wherever the plan is really waiting for the board to say something: a delay long enough to be safe is a delay that makes every run slower.

duration_ms.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds. Capped at ten minutes: a plan that must wait longer than that is waiting for something it should be reading instead, and an unbounded wait is how a bench ends up held by a run nobody is watching.

repeat.description: Run a nested subset of steps again and again, by count or by wall time. A reactor-level block step: it routes to no device, so it names none, and the reactor runs it rather than any device kind. The nested `steps:` list is the subset that repeats and has the same shape as the plan's own, so a `repeat` may contain a `repeat`. Devices stay open across iterations, a failed nested step aborts the whole run exactly as a failed top-level step does, and the run's result carries the records of every iteration beside the reason the loop ended.

count.description: How many times the nested subset runs. Reaching this count is a green exit. At least one of `count` and `duration_s` is required, because a plan may not loop unbounded; with both, the first bound reached ends the loop.

duration_s.description: How long the loop keeps starting new iterations, in seconds. Checked between iterations only, so a cycle is never cut in half and the loop always runs at least once; the elapsed time is therefore a floor rather than a deadline. Reaching it is a green exit. At least one of `count` and `duration_s` is required; with both, the first bound reached ends the loop.
